title: The Modern Devotion
hook: Dutch lay communities practice simple inner prayer; the Imitation of Christ comes from them

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bridget of Sweden, who buried her husband and began a larger life. Your line was a widow's second life. Whose new beginning did you help along? Day eight hundred twenty-eight.

Nobody in this narrow house in a Dutch town wears a habit. It is late in the middle ages. Nobody has taken vows. The men copy books by hand for a living, pool what they earn, eat at one table, and pray. Down the street, a house of women does much the same, sewing and spinning. On Sunday they all walk to the parish church like their neighbors. What sets them apart is quieter than that. They are trying to let the faith travel from the outside of their lives to the inside. The movement they belonged to came to be called the Modern Devotion. That's today's word.
screen: `NO HABITS, NO VOWS.` → `COPYING, SHARING, PRAYING.` → `FROM THE OUTSIDE TO THE INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Start with the man tradition puts at the root, Geert Groote, a preacher from Deventer who left a comfortable career and called people back to a plain, interior faith. Around him, laymen and laywomen began living together as the Brothers and Sisters of the Common Life, and others became canons in religious houses linked to the movement. Next, the method. Their prayer was simple. Read a little Scripture, slowly. Copy out a line that strikes you, keep it close, and return to it through the day. Look honestly at your own heart at night. No ladders of mystical stages. Just an ordinary day, turned toward God. Then, the book. From these communities came The Imitation of Christ, which tradition attributes to Thomas à Kempis, a canon of one of their houses. It opens with Jesus's words from John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "he that followeth me, walketh not in darkness." And then it turns inward again and again. Early on it says, in effect, that a humble knowledge of yourself is a surer road to God than deep learning. Finally, the direction: inward. In Luke, Jesus says, "the kingdom of God is within you." The Modern Devotion took him at his word. Not instead of the Mass and the sacraments; they kept those. Underneath them. The outward life mattered. The Devotion kept asking what was going on inside it. Copyists, weavers, schoolmasters, with ordinary jobs, doing one quiet thing on purpose every day.
screen: `GEERT GROOTE AND THE COMMON LIFE.` · `READ A LITTLE, SLOWLY. KEEP ONE LINE.` · `THE IMITATION OF CHRIST.` · `THE KINGDOM OF GOD IS WITHIN YOU.` · then, large: `INWARD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray simply. Choose one short line. Today's will do: he that followeth me, walketh not in darkness. Or any line of Scripture or poetry you already keep. Settle, and say it once, slowly, in your head. Then stay with it. When your mind drifts to the dishes or the inbox, don't scold it. Come back to the line, plainly, the way you'd turn back to a friend after a car horn in the street. If you pray, let the line become your prayer. If you don't, let it be a place to rest. The bell holds the time.
Modern Devotion. Lay communities in the Low Countries who practiced plain, inward prayer, and from whom The Imitation of Christ came. Today's word.
Your line: inward. Today, write one line from something you read on a scrap of paper, keep it in your pocket, and read it again once before the day ends. Day eight hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics still read The Imitation of Christ, often a chapter or a few lines at a time, and some keep it beside the Bible for daily spiritual reading or use it in retreats.

fork.setup: you're a young copyist in a Dutch town. you want to live your faith more deeply, but you have a trade and no call to the cloister. what do you do?
options: leave your trade and join a strict monastery.
share a house, work and prayer with others, and keep your trade.
decide deep faith is for priests and nuns, and leave it to them.
fork.reveal: the Brothers and Sisters of the Common Life did just this: ordinary work, a shared table, and simple inward prayer.

original.note: Latin: the modern devotion, the name the movement was given.

what a scholar hears: a movement that kept the church's outward forms and kept asking what was happening underneath them.

notes: Confirm Douay-Rheims (Challoner) wording of John 8:12 and Luke 17:21.

Imitation 1.3 paraphrased ('a humble knowledge of thyself is a surer way to God than a deep search after learning' in older English versions); not quoted because the translation is not on the validator's list.
Authorship of the Imitation is attributed ('tradition attributes to Thomas à Kempis'); scholars have debated it. Confirm phrasing.

Facts to confirm: Geert Groote of Deventer as founder figure, left a comfortable clerical career; Brothers and Sisters of the Common Life as lay communities without vows; canons regular (Windesheim) linked to the movement; brothers supported themselves by copying books; practice of keeping copied lines (rapiaria). No dates stated.
Original: 'devotio moderna', ecclesiastical Latin pronunciation; confirm.
